title: Is Chevron Stock A Real Bargain? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Chevron (CVX) stock trades at 15.3 times earnings, against 22.3 for the median S&P 500 company. The shares are that cheap even after returning 43.2% over the past year, compared with 13.7% for the S&P 500. A buyer could be getting a sound business on sale, or paying a fair price for profits that may not stay this high. So why is Chevron stock still this cheap after such a run? Chevron’s net income for the latest four quarters more than doubled from a year earlier, far faster than its share price, and that keeps the multiple low. The company earned $9.92 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, the latest quarter, nearly three times what it earned a year earlier. Revenue rose 35.4% from the same quarter of 2025. Chevron kept 17.5% of that revenue as operating profit, up from 8.9% a year before. The profit came with cash. Free cash flow over the twelve months to September 2026 equaled 8.3% of Chevron’s market value. Chevron generates that cash by pumping oil and gas in its Upstream business and refining crude in its Downstream business. Chevron earned most of its twelve-month profit in just two quarters, and that is the case for the discount. Of $32.9 billion in operating income over the twelve months to September 2026, $25.7 billion came in fiscal Q2 and Q3 2026. The latest year also stands out: Chevron’s operating margin for those twelve months was 14.6%, against 11.3% and 8.1% in the twelve months to September 2024 and 2025. On the October 30 call, management said oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel in the third quarter alone. It expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term. Chevron’s net income over the twelve months to September 2026 was $27.0 billion, and it has earned more before and seen it fall. Net income reached $34.2 billion in the twelve months to September 2022. The stock was then priced at just 8.1 times earnings. Today it trades at 15.3 times, nearly twice that. Net income fell in each of the next three twelve-month periods, to September 2023, 2024 and 2025. Management’s answer is more oil at low cost. Chevron plans to double production at its three Venezuela joint ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels a day of gross output by 2031. Management put the total cost of those barrels at less than $20 a barrel, far below even the third quarter’s lowest oil price. Company-wide output dips in the near term, though: Chevron said on October 30 that it expects its fourth-quarter upstream production to be 175,000 to 225,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day lower because of turnarounds and downtime. title: Chevron Is Doubling Venezuela Production. ExxonMobil Says It's Not in a Rush. Who's Right? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil remains cautious after Venezuela twice seized its assets. Uncertain long-term oil demand adds to investment risks. ExxonMobil's capital discipline could benefit long-term shareholders. Chevron(NYSE: CVX) plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela over the next five years, potentially more than doubling its oil production there to about 600,000 barrels per day. ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), meanwhile, isn't interested in rushing back into Venezuela. And quite frankly, I think ExxonMobil may have the better strategy. Chevron isn't starting from scratch. The company has operated in Venezuela for more than a century and maintained a presence, even as political instability and economic turmoil have driven other international oil companies away. In fact, in September, Chevron announced agreements providing improved fiscal, commercial, and legal terms for its Venezuelan operations. It also secured additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Management believes it can expand production while keeping total costs below $20 per barrel. Indeed, that's a pretty attractive proposition. Chevron already has infrastructure, local relationships, and operating experience. Expanding existing production is considerably different from building an entirely new business in a country with Venezuela's history. And if oil prices remain favorable, Chevron could generate substantial additional cash flow without taking on the same level of risk as a newcomer. Exxon has good reasons to be skeptical. The company has had its Venezuelan assets seized twice, most recently in 2007 under former President Hugo Chávez. CEO Darren Woods has indicated that Exxon would consider returning, but only with stronger legal protections and investment terms that justify the risks. I don't blame him. Venezuela's oil infrastructure needs substantial investment, political uncertainty remains high, and there's no guarantee future governments will honor today's agreements. And there's also reason to consider long-term oil demand. There are varying projections on this. The IEA projects that global oil demand could plateau around 2030. Wood Mackenzie has that plateau hitting in 2032. TotalEnergies(NYSE: TTE) has it between 2035 and 2040, while OPEC suggests "robust global oil demand growth prospects to 2050, with no signs of oil demand peaking over the forecast period." But even with OPEC's optimistic scenario, 2050 is only about 23 years away. Of course, even if demand levels off, existing oil fields will continue declining. The industry will still need replacement production. But if demand growth slows while producers keep expanding capacity, oil prices could face additional pressure. Under these conditions, spending billions on politically risky projects becomes harder to justify. Chevron's expansion isn't necessarily a mistake. Its existing operations, relatively low production costs, and improved contractual terms could make Venezuela a profitable source of additional oil production. But ExxonMobil doesn't have the same advantages. It would potentially need to commit substantial capital to rebuild operations in a country that has already confiscated its assets. The company has other places to invest, including Guyana and the Permian Basin, where it has established operations and greater confidence in its ability to generate returns. Overall, ExxonMobil's strategy just makes sense. Yes, Chevron could make plenty of money in Venezuela. But ExxonMobil is demonstrating that having the financial resources to pursue an opportunity doesn't mean you should. Sometimes the better investment decision is knowing when to walk away. title: What Mattered Most In Chevron’s Latest Quarter? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Shares of Chevron (CVX) rose 1.8% on October 30, 2026, the day the company reported fiscal Q3 2026 results, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. By November 6, the stock had fallen 8.1% from its close before the report, compared with a 4.4% decline for the index. Profit fell from the second quarter, yet it remained nearly three times its level a year earlier. So what is Chevron doing with the extra money? On the October 30 call, management said Chevron cut its debt by more than $3 billion in the quarter and added more than $4 billion to its cash. Buybacks did not rise alongside those moves. Management said the company kept its buyback rate at $2.5 billion to $3 billion and intends to stay within that range. Chevron bought back $11.1 billion of shares in the four quarters to September. On report day, Chevron’s advance slightly trailed the gains at Exxon Mobil and ConocoPhillips, which rose 2.2% and 2.7%. Over the past twelve months, Chevron’s free cash flow equaled 8.2% of its market value, while its dividends and buybacks together totaled 6.0%. The company is retaining more cash than it hands back, and its debt has declined. Total debt stood at $33.5 billion at the end of September, compared with $41.5 billion a year earlier. Has Chevron’s Bigger Profit Lasted More Than Two Quarters? Not yet. Chevron earned $2.21 billion in the first quarter of 2026, before profit jumped to $12.1 billion in the second quarter and settled at $9.92 billion in the third. On management’s own measure, adjusted earnings were $10.4 billion, down $1.6 billion from the second quarter. Management said upstream earnings fell on lower prices and lower volumes sold, while downstream earnings rose on higher refining margins and volumes. Chevron has earned profit this high before, and it faded. Since 2021, only the twelve months to September 2022, at $34.2 billion, brought more profit than the latest twelve-month stretch. Profit then fell in each of the years to September 2023, 2024 and 2025. Investors now pay 15.4 times the past twelve months’ earnings for the shares, compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500, and those twelve months include both big quarters. What Did Chevron’s Management Say About The Months Ahead? Management said Chevron will not change how it spends cash while prices swing this widely. Prices ranged from as low as $68 to as high as $132 a barrel within the third quarter, so the company is changing nothing in the short term, and growing the dividend stays its first priority. On refining, management expects margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. It also called refining and chemical margins very difficult to predict. Chevron said turnarounds and downtime would cut its fourth-quarter upstream output by 175,000 to 225,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. The fourth quarter brings one known charge. Management expects a transaction to close at the end of the quarter that takes $3.7 billion of debt off Chevron’s books and lifts its Bakken upstream earnings in 2027. Chevron will then report a one-time non-cash loss of $3 billion to $4 billion, a special item management said reflects only the accounting. With that loss set apart, the figure to watch when Chevron reports in January 2027 is fourth-quarter adjusted earnings, against $10.4 billion in the third quarter. title: One Unsettled Question Sits Under Chevron Stock - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Chevron (CVX) could lose some of what it earns from making fuel once a global shortage of refining capacity eases. During its October 30, 2026 call, management said 10% of the world’s refining capacity was offline at the time. Chevron’s own U.S. refineries, by contrast, ran a record amount of crude in the third quarter. You cannot yet tell how much of Chevron’s business is exposed to that shortage. A refining margin is the difference between what a refiner pays for crude oil and what it collects for the fuel it makes. Chevron’s refining operations sit in its Downstream business. Management said adjusted downstream earnings rose in the third quarter from the second because of higher refining margins and volumes. The whole company did not follow suit. Adjusted earnings fell by $1.6 billion from the second quarter, as upstream earnings dropped on lower realizations and lower liftings. A question about global supply, including how much capacity is offline worldwide, came up on that October 30 call. Downstream brought in $142 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, against $88.4 billion for Upstream. Segment revenue can include sales between Chevron’s own businesses, however, and revenue alone does not show what each business earns. Downstream revenue fell 9.8% that year. Across the whole company, the operating margin is now wider than a year ago. The operating margin reached 17.5% in the third quarter of 2026, up from 8.9% in the third quarter of 2025. Over the past twelve months it was 14.6%. That level is higher than at 34 of the 40 quarter ends since the end of 2016, so the company is earning near the top of its own ten-year range. Management has said it expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term. It expects those margins to moderate as refinery runs recover and export flows increase, a process management said will take some time. On chemicals, management put the share of petrochemical capacity offline at between 5% and 10%, and said margins will likely stay a bit elevated at least through the end of the year, maybe into 2027. Management also said that without some capacity closures and project deferrals, the chemicals market may return to oversupply as flows normalize. In both cases, management tied the easing to supply coming back. Chevron is adding capacity of its own, including roughly 15% more at its Pasadena refinery and another 7% planned at Pascagoula by 2030. These additions give the company more fuel to sell at whatever margin the market pays. In its fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, the figure to watch is whether Chevron’s downstream earnings rise or fall from the third quarter’s.
